scope: The structure of a cookbook guideline: its meta (frontmatter), title, summary statement, structured guidance, roled parts, named rules, the research each rule cites, its compliance section, its `triggers` field and its change history. Not this topic's: keyword case and the severity a rule's keyword gives a lint finding (sibling topic cookbook/guidelines/cookbook/authoring/requirement-keywords), and the `triggers` vocabulary (sibling topic activity-triggers).
research_type: How-to / troubleshooting (intent Do; domain technical writing; method practitioner and standards sources). Bar: product / how-to / definitional LOW-MEDIUM (broad independent consensus), no escalation.

questions.text: Best practices: what is current best practice for this topic?
Known solutions: what solutions, patterns, libraries and tools already exist, and how do they compare?
Platform guidelines: what do the platform owners' own guidelines say, for each platform the topic touches (Apple, Android, Windows, web, the databases and runtimes concerned)?
The expert's view: if we hired an expert consultant in this topic, what would they tell us: what to do, what to avoid, and what people usually get wrong?

methodology.method: guidelines/researching/process/research-methodology-and-sources: orient and classify the domain (technical writing; standards), go to the authoritative sources the brief names as this topic's platforms (IETF RFC 2119, RFC 7322, RFC 7991; W3C QA Framework, Manual of Style, WCAG 2.2, Process Document; Diátaxis; the Google and Microsoft style guides; the markdownlint, Vale and JSON Schema documentation), then requirements-engineering and guideline-development standards (NASA, IOM, AGREE II) for named, evidence-cited rules, and practitioner sources only for what no primary source covers. Every source cited was fetched; every quote is taken from the fetched page.
methodology.search_strategy: Direct fetches of the named standards and tool documentation; WebSearch for evidence-linking standards for guideline recommendations, single-source-of-truth documentation guidance and practitioner commentary on normative language.
methodology.inclusion: Primary specifications, standards and the tool owners' own documentation; standards bodies from adjacent rule-bearing domains (systems engineering, clinical guidelines) where the practice transfers; secondary sources only where no primary source speaks, said so in the trust basis.
methodology.exclusion: Keyword case and lint severity (requirement-keywords' research); the triggers vocabulary (activity-triggers' research); pages that could not be fetched (ISO/IEC Directives Part 2 returned 403; ACM Queue/CACM 'Kode Vicious' returned 403; NCBI Bookshelf returned a browser check).

summary: The standards that govern rule-bearing documents agree on the shape the draft describes: a required summary up front (RFC 7322 requires an Abstract, complete in itself), required metadata enforced by a schema (RFC 7322's required elements; JSON Schema `required` and `enum`; Astro and remark-lint validate frontmatter), requirements in one consistent, distinguishable style (W3C QA Framework Requirement 7), each requirement uniquely referenceable and expressing one thought (NASA), rationale kept with but apart from the requirement (NASA, Diátaxis, W3C), and per-version change documentation (W3C Process, Keep a Changelog). Evidence linked to each recommendation is a standard for trustworthy guidelines (IOM Standard 5.1, AGREE II), but at SHOULD strength, so the draft's MUSTs for the research folder and per-rule citations are unsupported at their stated strength. No outside source speaks to the cookbook's own role vocabulary, skill compilation, triggers field, compliance section or legacy exemption; those are recorded as prior-text claims for the owner. Missing from the draft: a conformance clause and scope (W3C Requirements 1-2), examples and notes marked non-normative (W3C Manual of Style, WCAG), one testable requirement per rule, the circumstances a rule applies in (IOM 6.1), identifiers kept stable across versions (W3C, OWASP ASVS), a single H1 and no skipped heading levels (Google), short lists (Microsoft), newest-first dated history (Keep a Changelog), immutable released versions (SemVer), rationale per rule (NASA), normative keywords only where required (RFC 2119), and automated checks (docs as code).
open_questions: Whether gf-research-folder and gf-rule-cites-research stay MUST: the strongest outside sources (IOM Standard 5.1, AGREE II) phrase per-recommendation evidence as 'should be provided' or as an appraisal criterion; the owner decides whether the cookbook's research-first ruling justifies MUST.

Whether gf-rfc-keywords stays MUST: the W3C QA Framework requires a consistent, distinguishable style for requirements (Requirement 7) and gives RFC 2119 keywords only as a technique; the owner decides whether the cookbook requires the keywords themselves (keyword case belongs to requirement-keywords).

Whether gf-roled-parts stays MUST: outside sources support labelling normative and informative content and separating reference, how-to and explanation at SHOULD/good-practice strength; the specific role vocabulary and the four required roles are the cookbook's own design.

Whether gf-title-heading (H1 equals the frontmatter title) is kept: no source requires it, and markdownlint's default (MD025 with front_matter_title) treats a frontmatter title as the document's top-level heading, so a title plus an H1 is reported as a second top-level heading unless the option is disabled.

Whether gf-compliance-section is kept: no outside source speaks to a section listing evaluated compliance checks; the W3C's conformance clause is a different element (what conformance requires), proposed as the new rule conformance-and-scope-statement.

Whether examples-are-non-normative is written as MUST NOT: the W3C Manual of Style says 'document editors must not make any figure, example or note normative' but also says 'No requirements for W3C publications are in this document.'

Whether normative-keywords-only-where-required belongs to this topic or to requirement-keywords: it is about when a rule carries an obligation at all (structure), but it is RFC 2119's own keyword guidance.
Whether keep-rule-lists-short applies to a rules part: Microsoft's seven-item limit is for lists in general ('if possible'), not for a rule-bearing document's rule count.
Whether the change history is ordered newest-first (Keep a Changelog) or oldest-first (the conventions.md example has one row, so the order is not stated).

Whether conv-* rules that state tool behaviour (conv-legacy-keeps-working, conv-role-values, conv-no-roles-under-reviewing, conv-roled-artifact-complete, conv-four-skills, conv-skill-names) remain in conventions.md as design statements without outside research, per owner ruling Q12.
limitations: Keyword case (uppercase vs bold) and lint severity are not researched here; gf-rfc-keywords is judged only on whether requirements carry a normative keyword at all, and its case clause rests on the sibling topic requirement-keywords.
The triggers vocabulary is not researched here; gf-triggers-field is judged only on whether a guideline carries the field and its list shape.
ISO/IEC Directives Part 2 (the ISO drafting rules on notes, examples and requirements) could not be fetched (HTTP 403), so the ISO view on non-normative examples is absent.

The ACM Queue / CACM 'Kode Vicious' column on MUST and MUST NOT could not be fetched (HTTP 403); NCBI Bookshelf's copy of the IOM standards returned a browser check, so the National Academies reading-room copy was used.
The per-recommendation evidence standards (IOM, AGREE II) come from clinical guideline development; their transfer to software-engineering guidelines is an inference, scored down for domain transfer.

No outside source speaks to the cookbook's own machinery: role values, compilation to builder/reviewer/verifier skills, skill naming, the research-exempt list or the `reviewing/` folder rule. These are recorded as prior-text claims, never as research findings.

Every claim has one citation whose page holds its quote, so every claim is `single`; corroboration across independent publishers is named in trust bases by claim id, not counted as multi-independent, because no two pages hold the same words.
WebFetch returns pages through a summarising model; quotes are the verbatim strings it returned from the page, and long pages (W3C QA Framework, RFC 7991, WCAG 2.2, W3C Process) were read in parts.
license: MIT (this research record); quoted material remains under its sources' terms and is quoted for verification.

claims.question: best-practices
claims.claim:
A roled guideline MUST give every part but the intro and the history a `role` in `artifact.json`, one of `rules`, `how-to`, `examples`, `review-focus`, `review-bar`, `build-bar`, `rationale` or `references`, and MUST have at least one part of each of `rules`, `review-focus`, `review-bar` and `build-bar`. It sets no `routes` and no `hosts/`, and does not live under `guidelines/reviewing/`.

What each role holds (`guidelines/implementing/data/indexing` is a worked example; its parts are `rules`, `look-for`, `a-complete-review-must-establish` and `a-build-must-establish`, among others):

| Role | Holds | Goes to |
|---|---|---|
| none (`intro`) | the summary statement | every skill |
| `rules` | the named rules | builder, reviewer |
| `how-to`, `examples` | how to keep the rules | builder |
| `review-focus` | what a reviewer looks for | reviewer |
| `review-bar` | what a complete review must establish | review-verifier |
| `build-bar` | what a complete build must establish: exactly one line per named rule, `` - `rule-name`: … ``, and no line naming anything else | build-verifier |
| `rationale`, `references` | why, and the sources | each skill's references |
| none (`history`) | the change history | none |

**Applies when:** any part of the guideline carries a `role`.

Each claim in `research.json`'s `claims` list is the per-claim record: `id` (kebab-case, unique), `question` (`best-practices`, `known-solutions`, `platform-guidelines` or `experts-view`), `claim`, `citations` (each with `title`, `author`, `publisher`, `date`, `url`, `accessed`), `source_type`, `quote`, `generated_by`, `query`, `trust` (`{"score": 0-100, "basis"}`) and `independence` (`multi-independent`, `single` or `uncorroborated`). The `verdicts` list gives each rule checked a verdict, `supported`, `contradicted`, `unsupported` or `new`, and the claims it rests on, at least one; every claim a rule cites MUST be named by a verdict.
